trust_decision.summary: Whether a peer-declared length may drive an unbounded allocation on the WebSocket read path. The published fix decides that only for the WebSocket frame header, by setting wsutil.Reader.MaxFrameSize in WSConnection.Read; the same decision is NOT made in Parser.Parse, where a SIP Content-Length reaches make([]byte, bodySize) with no bound, and Parser.Parse is exactly the parser the WS transport calls.

landing_point.why: The advisory summary names the WebSocket frame length, so an engineer opens WSConnection.Read; the unbounded allocation it guards is data := make([]byte, header.Length) at sip/transport_ws.go:400, and the published one-line fix lands in this same function at sip/transport_ws.go:364-365.

fix_sites.entry_point: Server.ServeWS (server.go:248) / Server.ServeWSS (server.go:253), reached from Server.ListenAndServe("ws") (server.go:147,163) and Server.ListenAndServeTLS("ws") (server.go:196-198); also TransportLayer.ServeWS (sip/transport_layer.go:265) and TransportLayer.ServeWSS (sip/transport_layer.go:288). Client side: TransportWS.CreateConnection (sip/transport_ws.go:269) and TransportWSS.CreateConnection (sip/transport_wss.go:45).

O3_reason_to_dismiss: For the O8 route: the advisory is scoped to WebSocket frame length, while a SIP Content-Length is a parser-level concern, and Parser.Parse already returns ErrMessageTooLarge for oversized input at sip/parser.go:254 and the TCP/TLS stream parser has its own Content-Length guard at sip/parser_stream.go:196 - so the route reads as already covered and can be argued out of scope.

O5_coupled_behaviour.what: The WS cap is the package-global ParseMaxMessageLength, which also seeds every Parser's MaxMessageLength (sip/parser.go:56) and is enforced by the TCP/TLS stream parser (sip/parser_stream.go:132,196). A fix that lowers or repurposes that global to bound WS frames silently shrinks the legitimate message-size budget for UDP/TCP/TLS, whose bodies that fit today would start being rejected; the per-transport knob a correct fix should honour instead is Parser.MaxMessageLength (sip/parser.go:46), and the fix ignores it in favour of the mutable global.

O6_input_shapes: one WebSocket frame whose declared 63-bit payload Length exceeds the cap (the guard is set once per Read call and applies to every opcode and to both client-side and server-side connections)
frames at or below the cap, including a message fragmented across many small frames, which the fix neither aggregates nor bounds

O7_producer.where: sip/parse_header.go:41-62 (header-name to parser map, content-length registered at sip/parse_header.go:56) and its value parser at sip/parse_header.go:173-177

O8_uncovered_routes.route: A WS text frame carrying a small SIP message with a huge Content-Length header reaches Parser.ParseSIP -> Parse -> make([]byte, bodySize) before any declared-body bound is applied, so the peer still controls a multi-GB allocation from a tiny frame.
O8_uncovered_routes.reason_to_dismiss: The advisory is about WebSocket frame length, not SIP Content-Length; Parser.Parse looks guarded because sip/parser.go:254 rejects len(data) > MaxMessageLength, and the stream parser already has a Content-Length guard at sip/parser_stream.go:196, so a solver can plausibly call this covered or out of scope.
O8_uncovered_routes.distance: 1 file, same Go package (sip); the WS transport reaches it at sip/transport_ws.go:250, which unlike the TCP transport never uses the guarded stream parser (compare sip/transport_tcp.go:227)

O8b_injection_room.sibling: An exported WSConnection.ReadMsg/NextMessage that assembles a whole SIP message from successive frame headers, allocating make([]byte, header.Length) itself.
O8b_injection_room.why_realistic: WSConnection is exported and already has WriteMsg (sip/transport_ws.go:447) with no read counterpart, so a maintainer adding message-level reads for SIP-over-WS would naturally allocate from the declared frame length and would need the same cap.

O8b_injection_room.sibling: A per-transport MaxMessageLength field on TransportWS/TransportsConfig that the frame guard honours instead of the package global.
O8b_injection_room.why_realistic: TransportsConfig is the documented per-transport configuration route and Parser.MaxMessageLength (sip/parser.go:46) already exists, so moving the cap onto the transport is the obvious next refactor.

O8b_injection_room.sibling: A TransportWSS that owns its own frame reader instead of embedding *TransportWS, so the cap has to be applied twice.
O8b_injection_room.why_realistic: TransportWSS already duplicates the dialling logic rather than reusing TransportWS.CreateConnection (sip/transport_wss.go:45-124), so a maintainer duplicating the read loop there is in keeping with the existing code.

O9_family: Uncontrolled memory allocation / resource exhaustion from an attacker-declared length (CWE-789, allocation with excessive size value)

O10_build.toolchain: go 1.23.0 with toolchain go1.24.2 (go.mod:3,5); single module github.com/emiago/sipgo, no vendor directory
O10_build.project_tests: No unit tests for sip/transport_ws.go at all; the only ws/wss coverage is TestIntegrationClientServer over loopback addresses (server_integration_test.go:98,100), skipped unless TEST_INTEGRATION is set (server_integration_test.go:83). Parser behaviour is covered by sip/parser_test.go and sip/parser_stream_test.go.

j.j_tempting_wrong_fix: Add reader.MaxFrameSize to the wsutil.Reader in WSConnection.Read (or reject header.Length > 65535 inline), confirm with a fat WebSocket frame, and stop - leaving Parser.Parse's Content-Length allocation, which the very same WS read path calls, unguarded.

out_of_scope_notes: The UDP transport calls the same unguarded Parser.ParseSIP (sip/transport_udp.go:227), but datagram transports are outside this WebSocket advisory's protection, so it was not pursued.
unverified: Could not read github.com/gobwas/ws v1.3.2 source (module cache is outside the permitted tree) to confirm that wsutil.Reader.NextFrame enforces MaxFrameSize before returning the header; the fix's effectiveness at sip/transport_ws.go:400 rests on that library behaviour.
